---
title: "Training word vectors"
subtitle: "Examine whether word neighbours indicate meaningful similarity"
description: "Learn how models train distributed word representations from local context. Examine why neighbour lists from a small corpus can be misleading."
categories: [similarity, word embeddings, inaugural addresses]
---

A curator wants to tag a speech archive without reading every paragraph. She
asks which words have similar vectors to `freedom`, `union`, and `peace` in the
collection.

A table of neighbours can appear meaningful. However, a word-vector model can
return a nearest neighbour for any word it retains.

A **distributed word representation** is one numeric vector per word, learned
from nearby words. This lesson loads one saved local model. It compares a
clearly related pair with arbitrary pairs.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

This lesson shows how to:

- read a saved word2vec skip-gram model with a fixed version
- examine the preprocessing and training settings stored with the model
- explain why the page loads a saved fitted model instead of training during rendering
- compare an expected related pair with random pairs
- summarize the full distribution of cosine similarities.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Load one saved word2vec model

Word2vec comes from work by Mikolov and colleagues on learning word vectors from
nearby words. The **skip-gram** version uses the current word to predict nearby
words within a specified window. The R package splits input on whitespace.
Before training, convert text to lowercase. Remove punctuation and numbers.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(quanteda)
library(word2vec)
library(ggplot2)

source("R/inaugural-corpus.R")

within_tolerance <- function(observed, expected, tolerance = 1e-4) {
  abs(observed - expected) < tolerance
}

metadata <- read_csv(
  "data/word2vec/word2vec-metadata.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    field = col_character(),
    value = col_character()
  )
)
metadata_values <- setNames(metadata$value, metadata$field)

paragraphs <- inaugural_paragraphs()
training_tokens <- tokens(
  paragraphs$paragraph,
  remove_punct = TRUE,
  remove_numbers = TRUE
) |>
  tokens_tolower()

model <- word2vec::read.word2vec("data/word2vec/inaugural-word2vec.bin")
embedding_matrix <- as.matrix(model)
punctuation_rows <- rownames(embedding_matrix)[grepl("[[:punct:]]", rownames(embedding_matrix))]

training_summary <- tibble(
  item = c(
    "training documents",
    "tokens after cleanup",
    "vocabulary rows",
    "dimensions",
    "punctuation rows",
    "unique word pairs"
  ),
  value = c(
    metadata_values[["training_documents"]],
    metadata_values[["training_tokens"]],
    metadata_values[["vocabulary_rows"]],
    metadata_values[["dimensions"]],
    metadata_values[["punctuation_rows"]],
    metadata_values[["unique_pairs"]]
  )
)

hyperparameter_table <- tibble(
  setting = c("algorithm", "dimensions", "window", "iterations", "minimum count", "threads"),
  value = metadata_values[c("algorithm", "dimensions", "window", "iterations", "minimum_count", "threads")]
)

model_fingerprint <- tibble(
  field = c("generator", "model SHA-256", "reproducibility note"),
  value = metadata_values[c("generator", "sha256_model", "reproducibility")]
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  training_summary,
  col.names = c("Item", "Value"),
  caption = "Training text and vocabulary checks stored with the saved word2vec model",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  hyperparameter_table,
  col.names = c("Setting", "Value"),
  caption = "Hyperparameters for the pinned local word2vec skip-gram model",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  model_fingerprint,
  col.names = c("Field", "Value"),
  caption = "Provenance for the committed word2vec model",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  nrow(paragraphs) == as.integer(metadata_values[["training_documents"]]),
  as.integer(sum(ntoken(training_tokens))) == as.integer(metadata_values[["training_tokens"]]),
  nrow(embedding_matrix) == as.integer(metadata_values[["vocabulary_rows"]]),
  ncol(embedding_matrix) == as.integer(metadata_values[["dimensions"]]),
  identical(punctuation_rows, "</s>"),
  length(punctuation_rows) == as.integer(metadata_values[["punctuation_rows"]]),
  as.integer(metadata_values[["unique_pairs"]]) == choose(nrow(embedding_matrix), 2),
  hyperparameter_table$value[hyperparameter_table$setting == "threads"] == "1",
  hyperparameter_table$value[hyperparameter_table$setting == "window"] == "5",
  nchar(metadata_values[["sha256_model"]]) == 64L,
  file.exists("data/word2vec/inaugural-word2vec.bin"),
  all(c("freedom", "liberty", "duties", "union", "government", "peace", "war") %in% rownames(embedding_matrix))
)
```

The metadata records 1,377 training documents, 134,419 cleaned tokens, 2,709
vocabulary rows, and 3,667,986 unique word pairs. It also records one punctuation
row, the trainer's `</s>` marker. Preprocessing removed punctuation before training, so
forms such as `peace.` and `peace,` do not become separate entries from `peace`.

Repeated fits used the same training code, seed, and `threads = 1L`. Each fit
produced neighbour lists in a different order. Similarity values changed by
about 0.03 here, but the ranking changed. This page loads one saved fit. The
metadata records its SHA-256 fingerprint, which identifies the file contents.
Keeping a fixed model file lets readers reproduce the exact printed neighbours.

## Print and assess neighbours

A nearest-neighbour list returns the words with highest cosine similarity to a
query word. Cosine similarity compares vector direction. Larger values mean
closer under the trained representation.

```{r}
nearest_words <- function(word, n = 6L) {
  predict(model, newdata = word, type = "nearest", top_n = n)[[1]] |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(
      similarity_band = case_when(
        similarity >= 0.8 ~ "0.80 or higher",
        similarity >= 0.7 ~ "0.70 to 0.79",
        TRUE ~ "below 0.70"
      )
    )
}

neighbour_table <- bind_rows(
  nearest_words("union") |>
    mutate(query = "union"),
  nearest_words("freedom") |>
    mutate(query = "freedom"),
  nearest_words("peace") |>
    mutate(query = "peace")
) |>
  select(query, neighbour = term2, similarity, similarity_band, rank)

expected_neighbours <- c(
  "texas", "attachment", "system", "jurisdiction", "confederation", "communities",
  "human", "evil", "mankind", "dignity", "civilization", "ancient",
  "friendship", "lasting", "world", "cultivate", "amity", "prosperity"
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  neighbour_table |>
    mutate(similarity = round(similarity, 3)),
  col.names = c("Query", "Nearest word", "Cosine similarity", "Cosine similarity band", "Rank"),
  caption = "Nearest neighbours from the pinned local word2vec model",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  nrow(neighbour_table) == 18L,
  identical(sort(unique(neighbour_table$query)), c("freedom", "peace", "union")),
  identical(sort(unique(neighbour_table$rank)), 1:6),
  identical(neighbour_table$neighbour, expected_neighbours),
  all(neighbour_table$similarity > 0.85),
  all(neighbour_table$similarity_band == "0.80 or higher")
)
```

Some neighbours look plausible, but a neighbour list always returns results.
Readable labels can make weak similarity evidence seem convincing. Keeping a
fixed file makes the printed words reproducible. It does not show that the
small model consistently gives related words higher scores than unrelated words.

## Compare a related pair with random pairs

The test compares `freedom / liberty`, a clearly related pair, with arbitrary
pairs. This choice provides an easy test for the model. If the pair barely
differs from arbitrary pairs, harder related pairs require more data before
readers can trust the results.

```{r}
cosine_between_words <- function(first, second) {
  first_vector <- embedding_matrix[first, ]
  second_vector <- embedding_matrix[second, ]
  sum(first_vector * second_vector) /
    sqrt(sum(first_vector^2) * sum(second_vector^2))
}

freedom_liberty_cosine <- cosine_between_words("freedom", "liberty")

set.seed(6101)
vocabulary <- rownames(embedding_matrix)
random_pair_indices <- replicate(
  1000L,
  sample.int(length(vocabulary), 2L),
  simplify = FALSE
)

random_pair_cosines <- vapply(
  random_pair_indices,
  function(pair) cosine_between_words(vocabulary[pair[1]], vocabulary[pair[2]]),
  numeric(1)
)

random_pair_summary <- tibble(
  statistic = c("mean", "median", "5th percentile", "95th percentile"),
  cosine_similarity = c(
    mean(random_pair_cosines),
    median(random_pair_cosines),
    as.numeric(quantile(random_pair_cosines, 0.05)),
    as.numeric(quantile(random_pair_cosines, 0.95))
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  bind_rows(
    tibble(statistic = "freedom / liberty", cosine_similarity = freedom_liberty_cosine),
    random_pair_summary
  ) |>
    mutate(cosine_similarity = round(cosine_similarity, 3)),
  col.names = c("Statistic", "Cosine similarity"),
  caption = "An expected related pair compared with 1,000 random word pairs",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  length(random_pair_cosines) == 1000L,
  within_tolerance(freedom_liberty_cosine, 0.7722, tolerance = 1e-4),
  within_tolerance(mean(random_pair_cosines), 0.7522, tolerance = 1e-4),
  median(random_pair_cosines) > freedom_liberty_cosine,
  as.numeric(quantile(random_pair_cosines, 0.95)) > freedom_liberty_cosine
)
```

The random-pair distribution overlaps the score for `freedom / liberty`.
In this saved fit the pair scores about 0.772, while random pairs average about
0.752. The model can still suggest words to examine, but a high cosine score
alone does not establish meaningful similarity.

## Show the similarity distribution

The distribution below uses every unique word pair in the cleaned vocabulary. It
also marks the `freedom / liberty` pair with a vertical line.

```{r}
normalized_embeddings <- embedding_matrix / sqrt(rowSums(embedding_matrix^2))
word_similarity_matrix <- tcrossprod(normalized_embeddings)
diag(word_similarity_matrix) <- NA_real_
word_similarities <- word_similarity_matrix[upper.tri(word_similarity_matrix)]
freedom_liberty_percentile <- mean(word_similarities <= freedom_liberty_cosine)

similarity_summary <- tibble(
  statistic = c("word pairs", "median", "95th percentile", "freedom / liberty percentile"),
  value = c(
    length(word_similarities),
    median(word_similarities),
    as.numeric(quantile(word_similarities, 0.95)),
    freedom_liberty_percentile
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  similarity_summary |>
    mutate(value = if_else(statistic == "word pairs", as.character(as.integer(value)), sprintf("%.3f", value))),
  col.names = c("Statistic", "Value"),
  caption = "Distribution of all pairwise word-vector cosine similarities",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  length(word_similarities) == as.integer(metadata_values[["unique_pairs"]]),
  within_tolerance(freedom_liberty_percentile, 0.4442, tolerance = 1e-4),
  within_tolerance(median(word_similarities), 0.7938, tolerance = 1e-4),
  within_tolerance(as.numeric(quantile(word_similarities, 0.95)), 0.9354, tolerance = 1e-4),
  freedom_liberty_percentile < 0.5
)
```

`freedom / liberty` is at the `r round(freedom_liberty_percentile * 100)`th
percentile of the full pairwise distribution in this saved model. The clearly
related pair has a score below the median for all pairs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-word2vec-cosines
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise cosine similarities among words kept by the pinned local word2vec model."
#| fig-alt: !expr sprintf("A histogram shows cosine similarities concentrated toward high positive values. A dashed line marks freedom and liberty at %.2f. The line is left of the median, not near the right edge.", freedom_liberty_cosine)
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"

source("R/lesson-figures.R")

plot_similarities <- tibble(cosine_similarity = word_similarities)

ggplot(plot_similarities, aes(x = cosine_similarity)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 40,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = lesson_colours[["context"]],
    colour = lesson_colours[["paper"]]
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = freedom_liberty_cosine,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    linetype = "22",
    colour = lesson_colours[["contrast"]]
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = freedom_liberty_cosine,
    y = Inf,
    label = sprintf("freedom / liberty\n%.2f", freedom_liberty_cosine),
    hjust = 1.08,
    vjust = 1.4,
    lineheight = 0.95,
    family = lesson_font,
    size = 3.6,
    colour = lesson_text_colours[["contrast"]]
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Many arbitrary word pairs score above a clearly related pair",
    subtitle = "Cosine similarity for every pair of words kept by the pinned word2vec model",
    x = "Cosine similarity",
    y = "Word pairs"
  ) +
  theme_lesson(grid = "y")
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  nrow(plot_similarities) == as.integer(metadata_values[["unique_pairs"]]),
  within_tolerance(median(plot_similarities$cosine_similarity), 0.7938, tolerance = 1e-4),
  freedom_liberty_cosine < median(plot_similarities$cosine_similarity)
)
```

Published embeddings use billions of training tokens. A larger training corpus
provides more contexts for distinguishing meaningful neighbours from accidental
neighbours.

## What to remember

- A word2vec model gives one vector to each kept word.
- The pinned model used skip-gram, 50 dimensions, window 5, 5 iterations,
  minimum count 5, and one thread.
- The word2vec package expects cleaned text before splitting on whitespace.
- Reproducing exact neighbour lists requires a fixed model file.
- In this saved fit, even `freedom / liberty` scores below the median of all
  pairwise similarities.

The curator uses the neighbour table to select passages for reading. The table
does not establish the archive's themes.
